items.title: DSA kya hai aur interview mein kaise use hota hai
items.one_idea: DSA is two things, a data structure (how data is organised) and an algorithm (the steps that use it), and an interview checks whether your steps still work when the data is huge: 10 lakh sorted names take up to 1,000,000 checks one by one but about 20 with halving.
items.spoken_hook: Interviewer ने पूछा: 10 लाख names में एक name, 20 steps में कैसे ढूँढोगे?
items.hook_source: carried-over LearnAI hypothesis, first DSA test; hookscore 46.5 WEAK, no DEALBREAKER
items.visual_idea: A long row of name tiles with a magnifier moving one tile at a time and a step counter climbing toward 1,000,000, crossed out in red; then the same row halved again and again, the counter stopping at 20; chips DATA STRUCTURE (the row) and ALGORITHM (the halving moves) land on the objects when named.

items.title: Big-O: steps ka growth, seconds nahi
items.one_idea: Big-O says how the number of steps grows when the input grows: one-by-one search grows in step with the data (10 lakh to 20 lakh names is 10 lakh to 20 lakh steps), halving adds one step, checking every pair quadruples when data doubles.

items.title: Space complexity: memory dekar time bachana
items.one_idea: Space complexity says how much extra memory an algorithm needs as the input grows, and the time-space trade-off is paying memory to save steps: finding a duplicate among 10 lakh numbers takes about 5 hundred billion pair checks with no extra memory, but 10 lakh steps if you spend memory on a set.
items.spoken_hook: Code अटक रहा था, memory बढ़ाते ही चल गया।
items.visual_idea: Two lanes: pair lines vs a set shelf; step and memory bars swap sizes.
items.everyday_anchor: A shopkeeper who keeps a price list on the wall instead of recalculating every price at the counter.
items.example: EXAMPLE (ran it, Python 3.12, counts not seconds): n(n-1)/2 = 499999500000 pair checks for 10 lakh ints (n=1000: 499500; n=2000: 1999000); set: 1000000 steps; getsizeof list 8000056 B vs set 33554648 B = about 4x (container only).
facts_to_verify: Do not claim set lookup is O(1) as a Python fact.
Show real printed counts; no exact bytes or seconds on screen.
Say the set costs O(n) to build and O(n) memory.

items.title: Arrays: memory mein kaise rakhe jaate hain
items.one_idea: An array keeps its elements in one unbroken block of memory, each the same size, so the computer finds element i with one calculation (start + i x size), which makes reading any element one step, while inserting in the middle must shift every element after it (about 5 lakh moves in a 10 lakh array).
items.spoken_hook: Array में दस लाखवाँ element, एक step में कैसे?
items.hook_source: direct_question is the one of the five types not yet tested (d001 interviewer_asked, d002 surprising_fact, d003 relatable_stake; company_specific needs a fetched company page we do not have); the answer lands in the very next line, no filler. hookscore 30.0 WEAK (Hinglish, calibrated on English), no DEALBREAKER seen.
items.hook_10s: Array में दस लाखवाँ element, एक step में कैसे? क्योंकि memory में array के सारे boxes एक के बाद एक, बराबर size के रखे होते हैं। एक छोटा हिसाब लगाओ और address मिल जाता है। [frame 0: a long row of equal boxes numbered 0, 1, 2 ... with a pointer jumping straight to the last box]

hook_candidates.hook: Array में दस लाखवाँ element, एक step में कैसे?
Array में element बिना ढूँढे कैसे मिल जाता है?
Array से पढ़ना एक step, बीच में डालना पाँच लाख।

items.visual_idea: A long row of equal memory boxes with addresses 0, 4, 8, 12 ... and a pointer that jumps straight to box 999,999 by one multiplication (start + i x size) while a magnifier crawling box by box is crossed out; then a new value inserted in the middle makes the boxes after it slide right one by one with a move counter reaching 5,00,000.
items.everyday_anchor: A row of lockers or seats in a cinema hall numbered in order: seat 40 is found by counting 40 seats from the first, you do not search each seat; but squeezing one new person into the middle makes everyone after them move one seat.
items.example: EXAMPLE (strategist ran it, researcher re-ran it 2026-10-22 with identical output, Python 3.12, counts not seconds): array('i') of 1000000 ints: itemsize 4 bytes; byte offset of index 0 is 0, index 1 is 4, index 2 is 8, index 999999 is 3999996 (offset = i x itemsize, base address aside); reading any index is 1 calculation; inserting in the middle of 1000000 items shifts 500000 elements, of 2000000 items shifts 1000000 (doubling data doubles the moves). The 4-byte int size is the printed itemsize on this machine, not a law; say 'for example 4 bytes'.
facts_to_verify: Address of element i = base + i x element size: Wikipedia array page gives 2000 + (i x 4) for 4-byte ints; say 'for example 4 bytes', itemsize depends on the machine (Python array docs).

Access O(1): Wikipedia (array: constant time store and select; dynamic array: indexing Theta(1)). Insert or delete in the middle O(n): Wikipedia dynamic array table. The page says plain static arrays do not allow insertion, so say 'inserting makes the elements after it move', as an array-like list does.

Python list is an array of references, so its boxes hold addresses, not the numbers themselves: NOT fetched this session (wiki.python.org TimeComplexity page gave only a redirect and its prose 'a list is represented as an array'); keep it out or say 'a typical list' only.
Do not say actual memory addresses or bytes from a real run on screen as a fact; offsets from the start are the formula. No seconds on screen.
Do not claim anything about how a particular language lays out multi-dimensional arrays.

CONFIRMED 2026-10-22 (researcher): Wikipedia Array page: elements same size, contiguous memory, address 2000 + (i x 4), select/store constant time; Dynamic array page: indexing Theta(1), insert/delete at arbitrary position Theta(n); Python array docs: itemsize is machine-dependent ('i' minimum 2 bytes, 4 here). Shift counts are n minus middle index by definition (array.insert moves the tail), not timed.
